en: Sutta Nipāta 3.6 Sabhiyasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now on that occasion Sabhiya the wanderer had been presented with questions by a deity who was formerly his blood relative:
“Sabhiya, you should lead the holy life in the presence of whichever ascetic or brahmin can answer these questions when they are asked of him.”
Then the wanderer Sabhiya, having learned those questions from that deity, approached those ascetics and brahmins who were heads of an order,
heads of a group, teachers of a group, well-known and famous founders of sects, esteemed as holy men by many people—
namely, Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Having approached them, he asked those questions.
Being questioned by the wanderer Sabhiya, they were unable to answer;
being unable to answer, they manifested anger, hatred, and resentment.
Furthermore, they questioned Sabhiya the wanderer himself.
Then it occurred to Sabhiya the wanderer:
"Those venerable recluses and brahmins who have assemblies, followings, and are teachers of groups; who are well-known and famous founders of sects, highly esteemed by the multitude—namely:"
Pūraṇa Kassapa …pe… Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta—
when questioned by me on these points, they were unable to answer;
being unable to answer, they manifested anger, hatred, and resentment.
"Moreover, it seems they are questioning me here.
What if I were to return to the lower life and enjoy sensual pleasures?
Then this thought occurred to Sabhiya the wanderer:
“This ascetic Gotama is indeed a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect esteemed as holy by many people.
What if I were to approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him these questions?
Then it occurred to the wanderer Sabhiya:
“Furthermore, those venerable recluses and brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of their journey, having reached old age, being elders,
long-established in the holy life, leaders of communities, heads of groups, teachers of groups, renowned and famous founders of sects,
esteemed as virtuous by the many— namely:”
Pūraṇa Kassapa... [and] Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta—when questioned by me on these points, they were unable to answer;
being unable to answer, they displayed anger, hatred, and resentment, and moreover, they even attempted to counter-question me here.
"But what will the ascetic Gotama say when asked these questions?
For the ascetic Gotama is young in years and a novice in his renunciation.
Then it occurred to Sabhiya the wanderer:
“A young ascetic is not to be despised nor held in contempt.
This ascetic Gotama, though young, is of great psychic power and great majesty; what if I were to approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him these questions?
Then the wanderer Sabhiya set out on a journey toward Rājagaha.

Wandering on his journey by stages, he approached Rājagaha, at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Sabhiya addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Full of doubt and perplexity,
desiring to ask questions about the tradition,” said Sabhiya.
“Be one who brings an end to these; being questioned by me on these questions, answer me in due order and according to the Dhamma.
“You have come from afar, Sabhiya.”
(Thus the Blessed One:
"To those who desire to ask questions,
I shall be the one who brings their end when those questions are asked."
I shall explain to you the Dharma in its proper sequence.
Ask me whatever question you desire, Sabhiya.
“I shall bring you to the end of each and every question.
Then it occurred to the wanderer Sabhiya:
“It is wonderful, indeed! It is marvelous, indeed!
That I, who could not obtain even a mere opportunity for an interview with other recluses and brahmins, have now been granted this opportunity by the recluse Gotama.
Contented, joyful, elated, and filled with rapture and happiness, he asked the Blessed One a question.
“What do they call a bhikkhu who has attained his goal?
(Thus asked Sabhiya) By what is he gentle, and how is he called tamed?”
"How is one called a 'Buddha'?
Being asked this by me, O Blessed One, please explain.
"By means of the path made by oneself..."
(To Sabhiya said the Blessed One:
"He has attained final Nibbāna, having crossed over doubt;
having utterly abandoned both non-existence and existence,"
Having lived the holy life and exhausted rebirth,
that bhikkhu is everywhere equanimous and mindful;
he does not harm anyone in the entire world.
The ascetic has crossed over, he is untroubled;
he is gentle, for in him no haughtiness exists.
He whose faculties are fully developed—
Having become disillusioned with both this world and the next, within and without, throughout the entire world—
that cultivated and tamed one awaits the time.
Having discerned all the aeons—
the cycle of existence with its two-fold passing away and rebirth—
one becomes stainless, free from blemish, and purified.
"One who has attained the destruction of birth—him they call a Buddha.
Then Sabhiya the wanderer, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, being satisfied, gladdened, elated, and filled with joy and happiness, asked the Blessed One a further question:
"What kind of one, O Brahmin, do they call a Brahmin?"
(Thus Sabhiya asked:
"By what and how is one a recluse? How is one a 'bathed' one?
And how is one called a 'Naga'?"
“Questioned by me, may the Blessed One explain.
“Having warded off all evils,
Sabhiya,” said the Blessed One.
Stainless, well-composed, and established in self,
having transcended saṃsāra, he is the perfected one;
unattached and such as he is, he is called Brahmā.
The one who has calmed the fires, having abandoned both merit and evil,
stainless, knowing this world and the world beyond,
has transcended birth and death.
Such a one is called a "samaṇa" because of being such;
having washed away all evils,
both within and without the entire world.
Among gods and humans who are subject to the cycle of existence, he leads through the kappa; him they call a "bathed one" (nhātaka).
He commits no offense whatsoever in the world.
Having severed all fetters and bonds,
he clings nowhere; liberated,
such a one is called a "Nāga" because of his suchness.
Then the wanderer Sabhiya... [as before] ...asked the Blessed One a further question:
"Whom do the Buddhas call the Conqueror of the Field?
(Thus said Sabhiya)
“By what and how is one wholesome?
And how is one called wise? O Blessed One, being asked, please explain to me how one is called a sage.”
“Having discerned all fields completely—
the divine, the human, and the Brahma-field,” said the Blessed One to Sabhiya.
Freed from all bonds rooted in the field,
the Conqueror of the Field is called "Such" because of his suchness;
having thoroughly examined all sheaths, he is liberated.
The divine, the human, and the Brahma-treasury—
all these treasuries, from their very root and bond,
he is liberated from; skilled and such-like, he is called "Thusness" (tathattā).
Having discerned both kinds of bright qualities,
with wisdom purified internally and externally,
he has transcended both the dark and the light.
Such a person is called wise because of being thus.
Having understood the Dhamma regarding both the non-existent and the existent,
both internally and externally, throughout the entire world;
"Worthy of worship by gods and humans, that sage has transcended the net of attachment.
Then the wanderer Sabhiya... [as before] ...asked the Blessed One a further question:
“What attainment do they call that of one who has reached the goal?
(Thus asked Sabhiya:
By what is he fully understood, and how does he possess energy?”
“How indeed does one become a thoroughbred?
Answer me this, Blessed One.
“Having discriminated all the Vedas in their entirety...”
(To Sabhiya, the Blessed One said:
"Of all that belongs to recluses and brahmins,
he who is free from passion toward all feelings,"
Having transcended all craving, he is a master of knowledge.
Having investigated the proliferation of name-and-form—
the root of disease both within and without— [he has understood it].
Freed from the bonds that are the root of all diseases,
such a one is called "Tathā" because of being thus;
he is detached here from all evils.
Having transcended the suffering of hell, he dwells in vigor;
being vigorous and striving,
the wise one is called "such" because of his suchness.
He whose bonds have indeed been severed—
the root of attachment both internal and external—
being liberated from all bonds that are the root of attachment, [is truly free].
“Such a one is called a noble steed because of his being thus.
Then Sabhiya the wanderer, having approached the Blessed One, asked him a further question:
“What kind of person do they call a learned brahmin?”
(Thus said Sabhiya:
"By what and how does one practice the noble way?
How indeed does one become a wanderer?"
“Having asked me, Blessed One, please explain.
“Having heard all phenomena and having directly known them in the world,” [said the Blessed One to Sabhiya].
Whatever there is that is blameworthy or blameless, they call him a true Brahmin—
one who has overcome all, is free from doubt, liberated,
and free from suffering, having transcended all attachments.
Having cut off the taints and attachments,
the wise one does not enter a womb;
having dispelled the threefold perception, the mire—
"He leads for an eon— him they call a noble one.
He who has here attained perfection in conduct,
being skilled, always understands the Dhamma.
He whose mind is liberated does not cling anywhere;
he who possesses the practice of conduct has no aversions.
Whatever karma exists that ripens as suffering—
Having wandered above, below, across, and in the middle,
practicing for full understanding,
one should abandon illusion, conceit, greed, and anger.
"He has made a limit to name-and-form;
him they call a wanderer who has reached his goal.
Then Sabhiya the wanderer, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, was uplifted.
Elated, uplifted, and filled with joy and happiness, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder,
and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
“Those which are three, and those which are sixty...”
O you of vast wisdom, having discarded the various doctrines of recluses—
which are based on conventional designations, letters,
and perceptions— you have crossed over the flood and reached the further shore.
You have gone to the end, you have crossed over suffering;
you are an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, I think, with taints exhausted— radiant, wise,
and possessed of abundant wisdom.
The maker of an end to suffering has carried me across.
Whatever I doubted, you have understood;
you have delivered me from uncertainty—homage to you!
O Sage, you have reached the goal along the paths of silence;
O unblemished kinsman of the sun, you are serene.
Whatever doubt I previously had—
The One with Vision has explained that to me:
"Truly, you are a Sage, a Perfectly Awakened One;
no hindrances exist within you."
And all those anxieties of yours have been scattered and laid low;
you have become cool and attained self-mastery.
Possessing fortitude and striving for truth—
listen to him as that Naga of Nagas,
the Great Hero, speaks.
All the gods rejoice,
as do both Nārada and Pabbata.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men!
Homage to you, O Supreme among Men;
in this world with its devas,
there is no one equal to you.
You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher;
you are the Sage who has overcome Māra;
you, having cut off all latent tendencies—
Having crossed over, you have ferried this generation across.
You have transcended all acquisitions;
your taints have been shattered.
You are a lion, free from clinging,
having abandoned fear and terror;
like a lovely white lotus, you are unsullied by the mud.
Water does not cling to it;
in the same way, you are not smeared by either merit or evil.
“Stretch out your feet, O Hero;
Sabhiya pays homage to the Teacher.
Then the wanderer Sabhiya, having prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as before] … I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, Bhante; may I receive full ordination.”
“Sabhiya, whoever who was formerly a member of another sect desires the going-forth in this Dhamma and Vinaya, desires the full ordination,
must undergo a probationary period of four months; at the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with his mind,
they grant him the going-forth and confer the full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu.”
"Furthermore, I recognize the distinction between individuals in this matter.

"Venerable sir, if those who were formerly members of other sects desire the going-forth and desire the full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya, they must undergo a probationary period of four months;
at the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with them—"
“They grant the going forth and confer full ordination into the state of a monk; I shall undergo the probation for four years;
at the end of those four years, may the monks, being pleased in mind, grant me the going forth and confer full ordination into the state of a monk.
Thus the wanderer Sabhiya received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One and received full ordination... [as before] ...
And so, the Venerable Sabhiya became one of the Arahants.
Thus ends the sixth discourse, the Sabhiya Sutta.
